teaser: Follow one shifter click from the cable to the chain, then see why different cogs make hills feel easier or harder.
title: How Bike Derailleurs Work
question: How does one click at the shifter move a bike chain onto a different gear?
idea: A derailleur guides a moving chain sideways between gears while a spring and two small pulley wheels keep the chain snug.

curiosity.intro: Trace the chain's loop, follow the shifter cable, and watch a small sideways nudge choose a new gear.
curiosity.carryForward: Keep looking for three jobs: guide the chain, move it sideways, and take up extra slack.

questions.question: Where does the chain travel?
questions.notice: Follow the chain around the front chainring, back to one cog in the cassette, and through the two small pulley wheels below.
questions.say: The chain forms one long loop. It grips teeth on a front gear, called a chainring, and on one back gear, called a cog. Turning the pedals pulls the chain and turns the back wheel.
questions.try: Use a finger in the air to trace the whole loop without touching the bike. Name the front chainring, back cog, and lower pulley wheels.

questions.question: What does the rear derailleur move?
questions.notice: Look below the back cogs for the small arm that lines its upper pulley with the cog holding the chain.
questions.say: On a mechanical bike, the shifter pulls or lets go of a cable. The cable and a return spring move the rear derailleur sideways. Its upper pulley guides the moving chain from one back cog to the next.
questions.try: Hold two hands apart like neighboring cogs. Move one finger sideways from one hand to the other to model the chain's short trip.

questions.question: Why are there two small pulley wheels?
questions.notice: See the chain bend around an upper guide pulley and a lower tension pulley before it heads forward again.
questions.say: Different cogs need slightly different amounts of chain. A spring turns the derailleur cage, and the lower pulley moves with it to take up slack. The upper pulley guides the chain toward the chosen cog.
questions.try: Curve a piece of yarn around two bottle caps on a table. Move the lower cap gently and notice how the extra loop becomes longer or shorter.

questions.question: Why do big and small back cogs feel different?
questions.notice: Compare the largest back cog with the smallest, then find the teeth that catch the chain.
questions.say: A big back cog is an easy gear for hills: the wheel turns less for each pedal turn, so the pedals need less push. A small back cog is a hard gear that can carry the bike farther per pedal turn on flat ground. With 32 teeth in front and 16 in back, the wheel turns 2 times for one pedal turn.
questions.try: With an adult, place the bike upside down on a flat floor or secure it in a stand. Turn one pedal slowly forward by hand while only the adult shifts. Watch the derailleur move the chain. Count teeth on the smallest and biggest back cogs, then count wheel turns for one pedal turn in an easy gear and a hard gear. Keep fingers away from the chain, gears, and spokes whenever anything is turning. No riding is needed.

reading.title: Six clues in one shifter click
reading.coverText: Follow the chain, cable, spring, and gears.
reading.parentNote: Age 8. Welcome spoken responses, pointing, sketches, and dictation; the scenic plates show the parts in context.
reading.foldableTitle: A little book of shifting clues
reading.foldableNote: Carry six gear-changing clues in a small book.

beats.title: A loop with teeth
beats.passage: Little traced the chain without touching it. The loop wrapped around a front chainring and one cog in the back cassette. Each gear had teeth that fit between the chain's rollers. When the pedals turned forward, the chain carried that turn toward the back wheel.
beats.prompt: How do the gear teeth help the chain carry a pedal turn?

foldable.heading: A loop with teeth
foldable.body: The chain loops around a front chainring and one back cog. When the pedals turn forward, the moving chain helps turn the rear wheel.

beats.title: A click pulls a cable
beats.passage: Big pressed the shifter once while the chain moved. The lever pulled a short length of cable. That pull moved the rear derailleur sideways. When the shifter let cable out, a spring drew the derailleur back the other way.
beats.prompt: What evidence connects the shifter click to the derailleur's sideways motion?

foldable.heading: Cable and spring
foldable.body: A shifter pulls or releases a cable. The rear derailleur swings sideways and guides the moving chain toward the next back cog.

beats.title: Guide it and keep it snug
beats.passage: Two small wheels turned inside the derailleur cage. The upper guide pulley lined the chain up with a cog. The lower tension pulley moved as the spring turned the cage. That motion took up extra chain, called slack, so the long loop stayed snug in every gear.
beats.prompt: How are the two pulley jobs different?

foldable.heading: Two pulley jobs
foldable.body: The upper pulley guides the chain. The lower pulley and a spring take up extra chain, keeping the long loop snug.

beats.title: A cage at the chainrings
beats.passage: This bike had two chainrings in front. A second derailleur sat above them. Its narrow cage surrounded the chain. As the cage moved sideways, it pressed the moving chain off one chainring so the neighboring chainring could catch it.
beats.prompt: How does the front derailleur move the chain without carrying it around?

foldable.heading: The front cage
foldable.body: On bikes with several front chainrings, a metal cage nudges the moving chain sideways from one chainring to another.

beats.title: The chain must move
beats.passage: Little noticed that a click did not lift a still chain onto new teeth. The pedals had to turn forward. Then each arriving chain link could meet the shaped teeth on the next cog and climb into place. A derailleur guides; the moving chain completes the shift.
beats.prompt: Why can a derailleur guide a moving chain but not place a still chain?

foldable.heading: Keep it moving
foldable.body: The chain must move forward to climb onto another cog. A shifter click alone cannot slide a still chain into place.

beats.title: Choose the useful gear
beats.passage: On the biggest back cog, one pedal turn produced fewer wheel turns and needed less push. That easy gear suited a hill. On a small back cog, the wheel turned farther for each pedal turn, making a harder gear useful on flat ground. Tooth counts tell the ratio: 32 front teeth divided by 16 back teeth equals 2 wheel turns for one pedal turn.
beats.prompt: Why does moving to a bigger back cog trade wheel turns for an easier push?

foldable.heading: Easy or hard
foldable.body: A big back cog makes climbing easier. A small back cog turns the wheel farther per pedal turn but needs more push.

math.title: Bike number crunch
math.intro: Add or subtract each set of bike numbers, regrouping ones and tens.

tasks.prompt: One parts tray holds 28 gear teeth cutouts and another holds 35. How many teeth cutouts are there in all?
tasks.hint: Add 8 and 5 first. Trade 10 ones for 1 ten, then add the tens.
tasks.worked: 28 + 35 = 63. The 13 ones become 1 ten and 3 ones, making 63.
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: A rider plans 72 pedal turns and has finished 38. How many pedal turns remain?
tasks.hint: Trade 1 ten for 10 ones. Subtract 8 from 12, then subtract the tens.
tasks.worked: 72 − 38 = 34. Regroup 72 as 6 tens and 12 ones, then subtract to get 34.
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: Two ride notes record 47 wheel turns and 18 more wheel turns. How many wheel turns do they record altogether?
tasks.hint: Add 7 and 8. Regroup 15 ones as 1 ten and 5 ones.
tasks.worked: 47 + 18 = 65. Add the regrouped ten to the other tens to make 65 wheel turns.
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: A box begins with 61 gear-number cards and 24 are used. How many gear-number cards are left?
tasks.hint: Trade 1 ten so 1 one becomes 11 ones. Subtract ones, then tens.
tasks.worked: 61 − 24 = 37. Regroup 61 as 5 tens and 11 ones, leaving 37 cards.
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: One bike outing lasts 56 minutes and another lasts 28 minutes. How many minutes is that in all?
tasks.hint: Combine 6 ones and 8 ones. Trade 14 ones for 1 ten and 4 ones.
tasks.worked: 56 + 28 = 84. Regroup the 14 ones, then add the tens to make 84 minutes.
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: A gear maker checks 93 teeth and marks 47 as finished. How many teeth still need checking?
tasks.hint: Trade 1 ten so there are 13 ones. Subtract 7, then subtract the tens.
tasks.worked: 93 − 47 = 46. Regroup 93 as 8 tens and 13 ones, so 46 teeth remain.
tasks.label: TASK 6

math.extension: Create another bike addition or subtraction equation with two two-digit numbers that needs regrouping.
math.printNote: Write one answer in each blank. Show how you traded ones and tens when you regrouped.
math.parentNote: Grade 2 math. Six tasks use two-digit addition or subtraction with regrouping and answers no greater than 100.
math.answerKeyIntro: Grade 2 math. Each problem regroups ones and tens; addition and subtraction are both included.

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: The shifter pulls or releases the cable; cable pull moves the derailleur one way, and the return spring moves it back the other way.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: The upper pulley guides the chain toward the selected cog, while the lower pulley and spring take up slack to keep the chain snug.

answers.label: Reading · 3
answers.text: The front chainring has twice as many teeth as the back cog: 32 ÷ 16 = 2, so the wheel turns twice per pedal turn.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Accept a spoken, dictated, drawn, or written explanation that links one derailleur part to its job.

quiz.title: Four shifting clues
quiz.intro: Follow the lever, cable, pulleys, and gears.

questions.prompt: What happens after a mechanical shifter pulls its cable?
choices: The back wheel leaves the frame
The chain stops needing gear teeth
questions.answer: Cable pull moves the rear derailleur sideways so its guide pulley can line the moving chain up with another cog.

questions.prompt: What does the lower tension pulley help do?
choices: Take up extra chain and keep it snug
questions.answer: The lower pulley moves with the spring-loaded cage to take up chain slack and keep the loop snug.

questions.prompt: How does a front derailleur change gears?
choices: Its cage pushes the moving chain between chainrings
Its pulley adds teeth to the cassette
Its lever turns the back wheel directly
questions.answer: A front derailleur's cage nudges the moving chain sideways from one front chainring to another.

questions.prompt: Which back cog usually makes a hill easier to pedal?
choices: Every cog feels exactly the same
questions.answer: The biggest back cog is an easier gear: the wheel turns less per pedal turn, so less pedal push is needed.

parentGuidance: A rear derailleur guides a moving chain between the cassette cogs, while its spring-loaded cage and two pulleys take up slack and keep the chain aligned. A front derailleur uses a cage to move the chain between chainrings. A large back cog is easier for climbing; a small one is harder and gives more wheel turns per pedal turn. For the observation, an adult should place the bike upside down on a flat floor or secure it in a stand, operate the shifter, and supervise every moment. The child may turn only the pedal slowly by hand. Keep all fingers, hair, and loose clothing away from the chain, gears, derailleur, wheel, and spokes whenever anything is turning. Stop all movement before counting teeth, and do not ride for this activity.
